text: You're the data engineer for Northwind Retail, a mid-size company selling through regional stores. Their nightly sales data currently sits in an on-premises SQL Server database, and it stays there — nobody outside the store back office can see it until someone manually exports a spreadsheet the next morning. The business wants that genuinely changed.

A real capstone starts the way a real project does: with a stakeholder's plain-language ask, not a technical spec. We need yesterday's sales, cleaned up and totaled by region and product category, sitting in our cloud database every morning before the eight AM leadership meeting. It has to run on its own. And our security team needs to sign off that no passwords are sitting around in plain text anywhere. Four sentences — every one of them a real technical requirement in disguise.

On-premises data means a self-hosted integration runtime, the only IR type that can actually bridge into that network. Cleaned up and totaled means a genuine mapping data flow — filter, aggregate, join — not just a raw copy. Running on its own, every morning, unattended means a schedule trigger paired with real error handling. And no exposed passwords means managed identity and Key Vault, end to end.

Five real stages, and every one of them maps directly to a chapter you've already completed: the self-hosted IR from Chapter Seven, a Copy activity landing raw data in ADLS Gen2, a mapping data flow transforming it, a curated Azure SQL Database table, and a Power BI report reading the finished result every morning.
The rest of this chapter builds every single stage of this diagram for real. Next: Connect and Build the Copy Pipeline — turning the top of this architecture into an actual, running pipeline.
